main.title: Mega Man Powered Up
main.subtitle: The first Mega Man becomes a toy box
main.summary: Mega Man Powered Up is Capcom's PSP platform game, first released in Japan on 2 March 2006. It rebuilds the 1987 Mega Man with rounded three-dimensional characters, new stages and additional playable Robot Masters. The familiar campaign still asks Mega Man to defeat Dr. Wily's machines and use their powers, but the remake enlarges what can be done with that foundation. A level editor and challenge mode turn the original's rules into tools for further play. Its small, expressive figures make the adventure look approachable even when the platforming demands careful control.

cards.heading: The first Mega Man becomes a toy box
cards.text: Mega Man Powered Up is Capcom's PSP platform game, first released in Japan on 2 March 2006. It rebuilds the 1987 Mega Man with rounded three-dimensional characters, new stages and additional playable Robot Masters. The familiar campaign still asks Mega Man to defeat Dr. Wily's machines and use their powers, but the remake enlarges what can be done with that foundation. A level editor and challenge mode turn the original's rules into tools for further play. Its small, expressive figures make the adventure look approachable even when the platforming demands careful control.

cards.heading: Play the stage through another machine
cards.text: Under the right conditions, Robot Masters can be unlocked as playable characters. Each brings a different ability into spaces originally approached with Mega Man's more general movement and attacks. A familiar obstacle may become easier, stranger or require a new route because the controlled character has changed. This gives the roster a practical role beyond the boss encounters. The player learns not only which weapon works against another machine, but how the whole platforming system feels when one of those specialised machines is responsible for completing the stage.

cards.heading: Build a challenge for somebody else
cards.text: The editor allows original levels to be constructed from the game's components, extending play beyond the supplied campaign. Challenge mode adds another set of focused tasks. Kazuki Matsue directed the project and Toshihiko Horiyama composed the music. Its compact character style reflected ideas that could not be realised in the same way on the original NES hardware. Reviews were positive, but weak sales ended plans for a similar Mega Man 2 remake. Powered Up remains a particularly expansive revisit, using the first game's machinery as the basis for both a campaign and a creative toolkit.

main.title: Nintendo DS Lite
main.subtitle: The Revision That Makes DS an Everyday Object
main.summary: DS Lite refines the original dual-screen handheld with a slimmer body, brighter displays and a larger stylus, while retaining its DS and Game Boy Advance game libraries.

cards.heading: 2006 / A redesign meets heavy demand
cards.text: The Nintendo DS Lite was announced on January 26, 2006, and showcased at E3 2006 the following May. The system launched in Japan on March 2, 2006. Heavy demand led to widespread shortages, and some retailers raised prices above list price. Nintendo shipped 550,000 units in March 2006, exceeding expectations, yet the console sold out quickly. To address demand, the company shipped an additional 700,000 units in April, but retailers were again sold out by late May. Shortages continued through much of 2006 and 2007.

cards.heading: A slimmer case, brighter displays and a larger stylus
cards.text: The Nintendo DS Lite is a redesign of the Nintendo DS. While retaining the original model's core features, it features a slimmer case, a larger stylus, improved battery life, and brighter displays. The top screen has a maximum brightness of 200 cd/m2, while the lower touch screen reaches 190 cd/m2. Its 1000 mAh lithium-ion battery provides approximately 15–19 hours of play after about three hours of charging. The DS Lite uses a different AC adapter from the original Nintendo DS and the Game Boy Advance SP due to a smaller power port on the top of the unit. The included stylus is 1 cm longer and 2 mm thicker than that of the original model.

cards.heading: Keeping the Game Boy Advance cartridge slot
cards.text: The Nintendo DS is backward compatible with Game Boy Advance (GBA) cartridges. The smaller Nintendo DS game cards fit into a slot on the top of the system, while Game Boy Advance games fit into a slot on the bottom. The Nintendo DS, like the Game Boy Micro, is not backward compatible with games made for the original Game Boy and Game Boy Color because the required hardware is not included and the console has physical incompatibility with Game Boy and Game Boy Color games.

main.title: Daxter
main.subtitle: The sidekick clocks in
main.summary: An exterminator’s job turns a familiar comic companion into the centre of a portable adventure.

cards.heading: Two years in another shadow
cards.text: Daxter arrived on PSP in North America on March 14, 2006, as Ready at Dawn’s first game. Set during the gap before Jak II, it follows the orange ottsel’s efforts to survive in Haven City and eventually free Jak. Working for an extermination business gives the adventure its own everyday absurdity: the former sidekick has to deal with infested buildings before becoming the rescuer remembered by the larger series.

cards.heading: Tools for an unlikely hero
cards.text: A swatter handles pests at close range, while a spray tank supplies both a weapon and ways to travel. Upgrades help Daxter cross gaps and reach new parts of the three-dimensional adventure. Jumping, climbing and extermination therefore share the same tools. Jamey Scott's score supports the comic setting, as the former sidekick takes the lead in his own PSP game.

main.title: Final Fantasy XII
main.summary: Final Fantasy XII is a 2006 role-playing video game developed and published by Square Enix for the PlayStation 2 in March 2006.

cards.heading: Battles and gambits in Ivalice
cards.text: Square Enix released Final Fantasy XII for PlayStation 2 in 2006. Players explore Ivalice and encounter enemies within its connected environments. The gambit system lets them set conditions for party members to act automatically in battle, while licenses determine which abilities and equipment each character can use. Optional hunts send the party after increasingly difficult monsters.

cards.heading: Dalmasca between two empires
cards.text: The game takes place in Ivalice, where the empires of Archadia and Rozarria are waging an endless war. The small kingdom of Dalmasca is caught between the warring nations. When it is annexed by Archadia, princess Ashelia creates a resistance movement. During the struggle she meets Vaan, a young adventurer who dreams of becoming a sky pirate in command of an airship. They are joined by a band of allies and rally against the tyranny of the Archadian Empire.

cards.heading: The Zodiac editions
cards.text: Final Fantasy XII earned several Game of the Year awards and sold over six million copies on PlayStation 2 by November 2009. Revenant Wings continued its world on Nintendo DS in 2007. The Japanese International Zodiac Job System edition reorganized character development; this version later formed the basis of the remaster The Zodiac Age.

main.title: Tetris DS
main.subtitle: Falling blocks meet Nintendo history
main.summary: Tetris DS is Nintendo's handheld puzzle collection placing the familiar falling tetrominoes beside characters and imagery from its earlier games. Standard play uses a Super Mario Bros. theme, while the other modes draw on series including Zelda, Metroid and Donkey Kong. The Nintendo DS hosts several variations on arranging blocks, with local multiplayer supporting a particularly large group. The collection gives the established rules a lively surrounding cast without losing the immediate purpose of fitting the next piece into a stack that must remain under control.

cards.heading: Falling blocks meet Nintendo history
cards.text: Tetris DS is Nintendo's handheld puzzle collection placing the familiar falling tetrominoes beside characters and imagery from its earlier games. Standard play uses a Super Mario Bros. theme, while the other modes draw on series including Zelda, Metroid and Donkey Kong. The Nintendo DS hosts several variations on arranging blocks, with local multiplayer supporting a particularly large group. The collection gives the established rules a lively surrounding cast without losing the immediate purpose of fitting the next piece into a stack that must remain under control.

cards.heading: The next piece changes the plan
cards.text: Standard mode continues the familiar cycle of moving and rotating a descending tetromino to complete horizontal lines. Each placement changes what the following piece can do, making the shape of the remaining gaps as important as the line just cleared. The pace rises as progress continues. Tetris DS also allows a piece to keep rotating before it locks, offering more time to reconsider a difficult position. The surrounding Nintendo animation supplies another visual rhythm, while the player's attention remains on the changing relationship between the current piece and the growing stack.

cards.heading: A handheld can host a larger contest
cards.text: Local play supports up to ten participants, while Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection originally offered online contests for as many as four. Competitive items add another source of disruption to the task of maintaining a clear playing field. The collection's six single-player modes provide alternative rules and themes when players want a different kind of puzzle. Together, these arrangements turn the cartridge into several ways of returning to the same set of shapes, allowing a solitary attempt to improve a score and a noisy group contest to share a recognisable foundation.

main.title: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion
main.summary: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a 2006 action role-playing game developed by Bethesda Game Studios, and co-published by Bethesda Softworks and 2K Games.

cards.heading: A journey through Cyrodiil
cards.text: The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is a 2006 action role-playing game developed by Bethesda Game Studios, and co-published by Bethesda Softworks and 2K Games. It is the fourth installment in The Elder Scrolls series, following 2002's The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, and was released for Microsoft Windows and Xbox 360 in 2006, followed by PlayStation 3 in 2007. Taking place within the fictional province of Cyrodiil, the game's main story focuses on the player character's efforts to thwart a fanatical cult known as the Mythic Dawn that plans to open portal gates to a demonic realm known as Oblivion.

cards.heading: Building a character at your own pace
cards.text: The game continues the open-world tradition of its predecessors by allowing the player to travel anywhere in the game world at any time and to ignore or postpone the main storyline indefinitely. A perpetual objective for players is to improve their character's skills, which are numerical representations of certain abilities. Early in the game, seven skills are selected by the player as major skills for their character, with those remaining termed as minor skills.

cards.heading: Making a world with daily routines
cards.text: Bethesda began work on Oblivion after Morrowind in 2002, aiming for tighter pacing and a stronger plot focus. Procedural tools helped create terrain, while high-dynamic-range lighting shaped its appearance and Havok supplied physics. Radiant AI let non-player characters make decisions and follow more complex routines. Fully voiced characters were a first for the series, accompanied by Jeremy Soule's music.

cards.heading: Expansions and later editions
cards.text: Oblivion received critical acclaim and several Game of the Year awards, with praise for the world, graphics and scheduled behaviour of its characters. Smaller additions were followed by Knights of the Nine in 2006 and Shivering Isles in 2007. The 2007 Game of the Year Edition gathered the expansions, and Skyrim followed in 2011. A remastered edition returned to PlayStation, Xbox and PC in April 2025.

main.title: Metroid Prime Hunters
main.summary: Metroid Prime Hunters is a 2006 action-adventure game developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS.

cards.heading: A message from the Alimbic Cluster
cards.text: Metroid Prime Hunters is a 2006 action-adventure game developed by Nintendo Software Technology and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS. It was released in North America in March 2006, with other territories later. The story takes place in between the events of Metroid Prime and Metroid Prime 2: Echoes. Players assume the role of series protagonist Samus Aran, who investigates a mysterious message that originated from the Alimbic Cluster and comes into contact with a legion of bounty hunters.

cards.heading: Hunters compete across the network
cards.text: The game contains more first-person shooter aspects than previous titles in the Metroid Prime series, emphasizing various multiplayer modes with Wi-Fi and voice chat capabilities. It introduced new bounty hunters with unique weapons and alternative forms as well as the ability to travel to different planets with Samus' gunship, concepts later expanded upon in Metroid Prime 3: Corruption. Hunters was announced by Nintendo at the 2004 Electronic Entertainment Expo. A pack-in demo version of the game, titled Metroid Prime Hunters: First Hunt, was included with the Nintendo DS when it launched in November.

cards.heading: Reception on Nintendo DS
cards.text: Reviews were generally favorable towards the game; praise focused on its gameplay and graphics, while criticism targeted its control scheme. It also received several honors; including an "Editors' Choice" award from IGN, which also named the game the "Best DS Action Game" of 2006, while Nintendo Power gave it awards for "Best Graphics", "Best Shooter/Action Game", and "Best Wi-Fi Functionality". Over 410,000 copies of the game were sold in North America in its first month of release, and it was the fourth best-selling game during its debut month in Japan. Metroid Prime Hunters was re-released on the Wii U's Virtual Console service in Japan in 2015, and in North America and Europe the following year.

main.title: Pokémon Ranger
main.subtitle: A different job in Fiore
main.summary: Pokémon Ranger is HAL Laboratory and Creatures' Nintendo DS action role-playing adventure about protecting people, Pokémon and their surroundings. Working in the Fiore region, the player completes a succession of Ranger missions rather than pursuing the usual Gym challenge. Wild Pokémon become temporary helpers whose abilities can remove obstacles or assist another capture. The handheld's stylus provides the central tool, the Capture Styler. A familiar collection of creatures is approached through a new profession, giving the player practical reasons to recognise what each one can do.

cards.heading: A different job in Fiore
cards.text: Pokémon Ranger is HAL Laboratory and Creatures' Nintendo DS action role-playing adventure about protecting people, Pokémon and their surroundings. Working in the Fiore region, the player completes a succession of Ranger missions rather than pursuing the usual Gym challenge. Wild Pokémon become temporary helpers whose abilities can remove obstacles or assist another capture. The handheld's stylus provides the central tool, the Capture Styler. A familiar collection of creatures is approached through a new profession, giving the player practical reasons to recognise what each one can do.

cards.heading: Draw the loop and watch the creature
cards.text: Capturing asks the player to draw consecutive circles around a moving Pokémon on the touchscreen. Its attacks threaten the Styler, so following the target is only part of the task: the next movement or warning also matters. Successfully completing the required loops recruits the creature temporarily. The direct gesture gives capture a different pace from choosing commands in a turn-based encounter. A Pokémon's position and behaviour become an immediate problem for the player's hand, with success depending on a sustained, careful movement around the screen.

cards.heading: Help borrowed from the landscape
cards.text: A recruited Pokémon can use a Field Move to tackle a barrier, break a rock, burn an obstruction or solve another environmental problem. After providing that help, it leaves the party. Poké Assists can also support a capture, connecting the creatures already befriended to the next encounter. These temporary partnerships encourage attention to the area around a mission. The useful Pokémon nearby is part of the solution, and using its ability changes the group of helpers available for whatever the Ranger meets farther along the route.

main.title: Ōkami
main.subtitle: The Brush That Turned Landscape into a Mechanic
main.summary: Clover Studio makes ink painting part of the action: Amaterasu draws symbols with the Celestial Brush to fight, solve puzzles and restore a corrupted landscape.

cards.heading: Amaterasu and a painted Japan
cards.text: Capcom released Clover Studio's ?kami for PlayStation 2 in Japan on April 20, 2006. The player guides Amaterasu through a mythic Japan whose landscapes have lost their color under a spreading corruption. Its painted appearance carries into the controls: the Celestial Brush pauses the action so the player can draw symbols over the scene, cutting objects, creating wind and restoring life.

cards.heading: Drawing with the Celestial Brush
cards.text: A line drawn with the Celestial Brush can cut an object; a circle can bring out the sun. Other symbols summon wind or water and restore damaged parts of the world. Learning these gestures opens new solutions in combat, exploration and puzzles. The player briefly steps out of the moving scene to change it with a brushstroke, then returns to the action to see the result.

cards.heading: Ink painting in motion
cards.text: Ink outlines, clouds, flowing water and vegetation give ?kami an appearance inspired by sumi-e, prints and calligraphy. These marks also have to show the player where to go and what can be reached. The three-dimensional world keeps its painted character as Amaterasu moves through it, with effects and scenery following the same visual language as the brush controls.

cards.heading: The return of color
cards.text: Purifying an area brings a surge of color and vegetation. Trees blossom, grass grows and the sky changes as the landscape recovers. The transformation shows the result of Amaterasu's work in places the player will continue to explore. Restoring each area changes both its appearance and the experience of returning to it.

main.title: New Super Mario Bros.
main.summary: New Super Mario Bros. returns Mario to side-scrolling platforming on Nintendo DS. Familiar transformations and an expanded moveset carry him through eight worlds in search of Princess Peach.

cards.heading: New Super Mario Bros.
cards.text: New Super Mario Bros. brought a new side-scrolling Mario adventure to Nintendo DS in 2006. Across eight worlds and more than eighty levels, Mario pursues Bowser Jr. and Bowser to rescue Princess Peach. Familiar power-ups include the Super Mushroom, Fire Flower and Super Star, while an expanded moveset and new transformations supply other ways through the stages. It began the New Super Mario Bros. subseries, reaching North America and Japan in May before Europe and Australia in June.

cards.heading: Reception and legacy
cards.text: New Super Mario Bros. released with critical and commercial success, with many considering it as the main contributor in the revival of the 2D platforming genre. Praise went towards the game's improvements and introductions made to the Mario franchise, level design, faithfulness to older Mario games, and its graphics and audio; while minor criticism was targeted at its low difficulty level and lingering similarities to previous games. It received numerous awards and was called one of the best games available for the Nintendo DS by many critics, with some further calling it one of the best side-scrolling Super Mario titles. It sold over 30 million copies worldwide, making it the best-selling game for the Nintendo DS and one of the best-selling video games of all time. The game's success led to a line of sequels and follow-ups, starting with New Super Mario Bros. Wii (2009).
